[0:00 · ~30s] Say nothing. No introduction. Walk the room and hand every person a paper copy of the memo (arrestInstructions.jpg). Hand it over the way a desk sergeant would hand out the night's assignment: no eye contact, next. When the last copy is out, advance.

What is your assignment?

[0:30 · ~2 min] Let the room work it out. Expect phones out: Google Lens, ChatGPT, someone who reads a little Dutch or German. Let them. That is the point; hold it for the end of the talk. What they should land on, item by item: 1. Report to the canteen at 5:45. Turn out at 6:30. Cars for the outlying districts. Patrols of detectives, two house searches each. 2. Search for literature of the International Bible Students Association, "better known as Jehovah's Witnesses": books, brochures, leaflets, and Bibles with notes written in them, especially in Isaiah, Daniel and Revelation. 3. Seize it. Detain the occupant. Take them to the nearest station and phone the Central Bureau, extension 273 or 274. 4. Nothing found? The occupant signs a form in triplicate. Refuses? Arrest them too. 5–6. Prisoners carry their identity card and are held in the basement of the Central Bureau. Seized material is labelled and handed in at room 20. Facts if asked: typed instruction from the Rotterdam police Centraal Bureau, Inlichtingendienst (intelligence service). Undated, unsigned, folded in four, kept in the family papers. The mention of the persoonsbewijs (the occupation ID card) and Geert leaving the force in April 1943 put it at about 1941–43. Ask: did anyone notice the last line? Then advance.
The last line

“P.S. Afterwards there is coffee in the canteen.”

How does that make you feel?

[2:30 · ~1 min] Read the translation out loud, slowly. Then ask the question and wait. Take two or three answers. Things people usually say: it's ordinary, it's office life, it's the same tone as a team-lunch email. Arresting your neighbours at dawn for owning an annotated Bible, and then coffee. This is a real piece of paper from my family. It belonged to my great-grandfather, Geert Greydanus, a detective in Rotterdam. I don't know whether he went on this raid. What I do know is what he did when the order was Jews instead.
How I came to have it

A box of family papers

  • I was born in Canada. So were my parents.
  • All four of my grandparents emigrated from the Netherlands after the Second World War.
  • I knew, vaguely, that my mother's family had been in a concentration camp called Vught.
  • I don't speak Dutch.
[3:30 · ~1 min] Personal, short. The memo came out of a box of family possessions, with a lot of other papers: letters, forms, a journal, camp scrip, ID cards. Born in Canada, parents born in Canada, all four grandparents came over after the war. The family story was a sentence, not a story: "they were in Vught." Nobody really talked about it. And I couldn't read the papers myself.
About 2010

I typed “Geert Greydanus” into Google

It's an unusual spelling, and it came back with real results.

  • Almost all of it was in Dutch.
  • The papers at home were handwritten, German or Dutch, torn, taped and stained.
  • He spelled his own name three ways: Greydanus, Greijdanus, Greidanus.
[4:30 · ~45s] Around 2010 I googled the name, and because the spelling is unusual, the hits were actually him: archives, a Dutch newspaper list, museum pages. But it was in Dutch, and the papers at home were worse: handwriting, German, carbon copies, things taped back together. Even the name isn't stable. The records use Greydanus, Greijdanus and Greidanus; Gerrit was his cover name. That alone breaks naive search. Let me show you what I mean. One slide each, quickly.
28 April 1943
Dismissal from the police

“…dat U op 9 April 1943 niet in dienst bent verschenen voor het arresteeren van Joden.”…that on 9 April 1943 you did not report for duty to arrest Jews.

Document 1 of 5
[5:15 · ~25s] Typed, official, from the office of the Director-General of Police. Dismissed for "unsuitability", because on 9 April 1943 he did not report for duty to arrest Jews. That sentence is the whole story in one line, and it took me years to read it.
6 December 1943
A letter home from Kamp Vught

“Moeder, Gerard en Corrie hebben nr. 0666.”Mother, Gerard and Corrie have no. 0666.

Document 2 of 5
[5:40 · ~25s] Camp stationery: the camp rules are printed at the top. Written by his daughter Wietske, 19, prisoner 0667, Block 24. She asks for food and sweaters for her brothers and explains the rules: one letter every two weeks, one parcel per person per week. Her mother and the two youngest boys share number 0666. Why a 19-year-old was in a camp is coming up.
About 22 June 1944
An appeal to the Reichskommissar, in German

“Seit etwa 9 Wochen befindet sich mein Vater G. G. im Konzentrationslager Vught, ohne dass wir etwas von ihm gehört haben.”For about 9 weeks my father G. G. has been in Vught concentration camp, without our hearing anything from him.

Document 3 of 5
[6:05 · ~25s] A pencil draft in German to Seyss-Inquart, the Nazi governor of the Netherlands, written about nine weeks after Geert's arrest by one of his children ("mein Vater"), on the back of a business form. The camp said he was in a section with no numbers; a parcel came back "without further notice". "May he not send news home?" Undated, unsigned. The family had German from Johanna, who grew up near the Ruhr mines. Also in the journal: a torn scrap in Geert's pencil from August 1944, "Provisional destination: Kleve. After that onward, don't know where to. I am brave."

Buchenwald prisoner no. 5892

“Beruf: Polizeibeamter … Verhaftet am: 20.4.1944, wo: Varsseveld”Occupation: police officer. Arrested 20 April 1944, Varsseveld.

[6:30 · ~25s] From the Arolsen Archives, not the box. The camp's intake form: occupation police officer, married, five children, height 179, hard of hearing, teeth missing. Arrested 20 April 1944 at Varsseveld, delivered by the SD in The Hague. Signed at the bottom by Geert.

“Which fellow prisoners do you know who died?”

“De fam. Rohaan – Heynen – v. Braak en Berlijn zijn door mij persoonlijk bezocht.”I personally visited the Rohaan, Heynen, Van Braak and Berlijn families.

Document 5 of 5
[6:55 · ~30s] This is the one that looks like the TV evidence board: torn, taped, stained. A post-war Red Cross questionnaire. Asked to name fellow prisoners who died in captivity, he lists fourteen men from memory, with guessed ages and towns, plus two who were moved to other camps. Then: "I personally visited the families." Every one of those names became a thread to pull.
The goal

Make it readable. Preserve it online. For our grandchildren, and for any other family that stumbles across the same names.

[7:25 · ~30s] That was the goal from the start. Get it out of a box and out of Dutch. Make it last. And make it findable, because every one of those fourteen men has a family too, and some of them are googling their grandfather's name right now.
Off and on, until 2020

It looked like a TV detective's wall

Which details matter? Which are accurate? Which two names are really one person?

[7:55 · ~45s] Leading up to 2020 I picked it up on and off. It was the scene from every detective show: documents, sticky notes, strings. The hard part isn't reading one document. It's that the stories intersect. Every item on this sketch is a real problem from the archive: "Oom Geert" was Geert's nickname, but "Oom Gert" was a different resistance leader in the same district, arrested the same day. One Red Cross letter says he was arrested 4 April; every other source says 20 April. One form says he went to Buchenwald via Krefeld; four say Kleve. You can't tell which details matter, or which are wrong, until you've held all of them at once.

[8:40 · ~1 min] Seven years later, three weeks ago, my son asked to use the papers for a school project. I thought: I already pay for Claude. Let's just throw everything at it. It started as a Claude Doc and became a GitHub repo and a GitHub Pages site, with a map, a timeline, a PDF, and a local copy of every source it cites. Numbers as of 15 Nov 2026: about 240 archived source files (84 family scans and transcriptions, about 128 web sources, 29 archive documents), repo created 10 Nov, 91 commits, 27 PRs. Credit where due: it builds on Jurjen Hoekstra's years of research and his 2020 booklet. Now, the story, as we can tell it today.
Geert Greydanus · 1899–1965

A Rotterdam detective who didn't show up

  • 1 Dec 1899 Born in Kubaard, Friesland, second of nine children. Farm work from about age 10.
  • by 1940 A senior detective with Rotterdam's Centrale Recherche, after service in the military police.
  • 9 Apr 1943 Ordered to round up Rotterdam's last Jews. Orders are now compulsory. He doesn't report, and goes into hiding.His wife and five children stay behind, at the address the police have on file.

Rotterdam policemen were called in that evening. “TWEE … weigerden.” Two refused.Vrij Nederland (underground paper), 15 May 1943

[9:40 · ~45s] Born 1 December 1899 in Friesland. Military police, then the Rotterdam police; by 1940 a senior detective, "majoor" in some records, brigadier in others (the sources genuinely disagree on rank). Early 1943, police leadership makes taking part in German-ordered actions compulsory, on pain of dismissal. On the evening of 8–9 April 1943 the force is called in to arrest Jews. Geert and one other detective, Nicolaas van Velzen, don't come. Both go into hiding; neither tells his wife where. The underground paper Vrij Nederland reported it a month later: of the men called in, two refused. (The paper's own figure of 1,000 is left off the slide because nothing independent confirms it.) That's the first public account, written at the time and independent of the family. And note what going into hiding meant: his wife and five children were still at home, at the address on file.
April 1943 – April 1944

“Oom Geert” wasn't sitting around

  • A year on Hendrik Satter's farm near Varsseveld, as “Oom Geert” (Uncle Geert).
  • Able-bodied, a police uniform, police experience.
  • Placing people in hiding, moving downed Allied airmen, distributing illegal newspapers.
  • He made sure as little as possible was written down.Interrogation was a real threat to everyone he knew.
[10:25 · ~40s] First a few days in Rotterdam, then Winterswijk, then a year on the Satter family farm at Sinderen, near Varsseveld. The farm was a resistance hub: the underground newspaper Trouw was planned there, and sometimes more than 30 people were hiding on it. His cover name, from his own signed form after the war: "de Boer Gerrit, born 1-9-97, Leeuwarden" — deliberately close to his real details, easy to remember under questioning. He had a false Rotterdam police ID. He told his son Ben he worked as the underground's "internal detective", tracing who was skimming stolen ration coupons. Very little of this is on paper, and that was the point: anything written down could be beaten out of someone.
1–18 December 1943

His family is taken hostage

  • Johanna and all five children are taken to Kamp Vught.
  • German policy: arrest the families of police who went into hiding. About 150 relatives were held.
  • Geert panics and wants to turn himself in. Hendrik Satter and Anne Schaap talk him out of it.
  • 18 Dec Released, “in view of the coming Christmas season”.Rauter, the SS police chief, claimed the desertions had stopped. It had worked.
[11:05 · ~50s] On 1 December 1943 Johanna and all five children were taken: questioned, then sent to Kamp Vught. Johanna and Wietske got numbers in the women's camp, the two teenage boys in the men's camp, the two youngest no numbers at all. The Vught index cards say: arrived 2 Dec 1943, released 18 Dec 1943. "Gijz." on the card means gijzelaar, hostage. This was SS police chief Rauter's policy: arrest the families of policemen who went into hiding with their pistols. If the officer reported within four weeks, the family was freed and he went to a concentration camp. About 150 relatives of police officers were held in Vught this way. Van Velzen's family too. Geert panicked and wanted to give himself up. Hendrik Satter and Anne Schaap, who was engaged to Satter's daughter, talked him out of it and moved him to Friesland for a few weeks. On 18 December Rauter released the families "in view of the coming Christmas season", to their surprise. His note says police desertion had "stopped entirely". He offered the men their jobs back if they reported by 3 January. Geert didn't.
20 April 1944

He went back for his belongings

  • Geert had already moved to Friesland. He came back to the Satter farm for a weekend, to fetch his things.
  • That day the SD struck across the whole Achterhoek, guided by Willy Markus, an informer who had spent three months inside the resistance.
  • Geert, Hendrik Satter and Anne Schaap were taken from the farm.
27
prisoners sent on to Vught the next day
22
men shot in the dunes at Overveen, 6 June 1944
“zwartste dag”
“the blackest day for the Achterhoek resistance” (Het Grote Gebod)
[11:55 · ~40s] Spring 1944: he's been sent to work for the Trouw group in Friesland. About a week later he comes back to Varsseveld for a weekend to get his belongings, and walks into the worst day of the war in that district. (Ben says he had a premonition and threw his revolver and false IDs into the outhouse.) Willy Markus, a café owner turned paid SD informer, had won the trust of the local fighting groups. On 20 April 1944 he struck: raids in Neede, Eibergen, Borculo, Lichtenvoorde, Varsseveld, Aalten. The local resistance report: "On April 20, 1944, he struck. On that date, 3 persons were taken away here, namely Satter, Greydanus, and Schaap." Sources differ on counts: Wikipedia NL and Westland give 27 prisoners to Vught the next day, about half of whom died; 22 men were shot at Overveen on 6 June. Markus got life, reduced to 18 years.
21 April – 9 August 1944

Almost four months in the Vught bunker

  • The camp prison: cell 117, then cell 93. Interrogated and tortured.
  • He held to one story: a policeman who refused to arrest Jews. Not a resistance man.
  • The men taken with him went before a German police court. Most were executed.Overveen 6 June · Fort Rhijnauwen 25 July · Vught itself in August
  • Geert was classed as a political prisoner instead, and put on a train to Germany.
  • After the war he named 14 fellow prisoners who had died, and visited their families.
[12:35 · ~45s] Nearly four months in the bunker, the prison inside the camp. The Red Cross summary of his own statements: cell 117 until early July, then cell 93. Survivors name the interrogators and a guard called "Popeye" who crept along the cells in sneakers. He held to his story: he was a policeman who refused to arrest Jews and went into hiding, nothing more. The men arrested in the same sweep, many tied to weapons and the fighting groups, were sentenced by the police court and shot. He was classified a political prisoner and sent on. Careful with wording here: the 14 names are from his Red Cross form in August 1945 — fellow prisoners he knew had died, whose families he then visited. They are not people he gave up under interrogation. No source says he betrayed anyone. In his own post-war forms he played the torture down: "not such that I suffered from it physically for long." The family understood it differently.
August 1944 – March 1945

Buchenwald, then forced labour

  • 9 Aug 1944 Train to the prison at Kleve, with 15 others.
  • 15 Aug 1944 Registered at Buchenwald, prisoner 5892, in the overcrowded “Little Camp”.
  • 4 Sep 1944 One of 100 men sent to set up the Niederorschel subcamp: Junkers aircraft wings, 12-hour shifts, six days a week.
  • Oct 1944 Joined by hundreds more, among them Leo Palache, 18, a Dutch Jew whose parents had just been murdered at Auschwitz.
[13:20 · ~30s] Out of Vught on 9 August, via Kleve, registered at Buchenwald on 15 August as political prisoner 5892. Three weeks later he's one of the first hundred men to set up the Niederorschel subcamp, about 700 prisoners in the end, building aircraft wings on an assembly line: "every 30 minutes the bell rings and the wing moves up". His youngest son Ben was born in Rotterdam on 6 October 1944, while he was there. Leo Palache arrived from Auschwitz at the end of October. Remember that name.
1–10 April 1945

The death march back to Buchenwald

10
days on foot, from Easter Sunday
120–150
km through Thuringia
527
prisoners set out
425
arrived

“People falling behind shot and left … dead in the gutter.”Steven Fenves, who walked in the same column, aged 13 (USHMM oral history, 2005)

[13:50 · ~40s] Easter Sunday, 1 April 1945. The front is coming; the camp is evacuated. Ten days on foot, roughly 120–150 km. Barbed wire set up around the column every night. Anyone who fell behind was shot. Numbers: the Thuringian forced-labour museum says 527 set out and 425 arrived; Hoekstra says 525 set out and more than 100 died. Geert's own form is two lines: "a journey on foot through Thuringia, a great many difficulties", and of the Dutch group, Akker of Leeuwarden died on the way; "the others all came back". The family account (Ben, and Wietske via her daughter): Geert and a Catholic political prisoner, almost certainly Anton Schepen, dragged Leo Palache along. Leo's own 1995 testimony describes wounded feet and dragging himself, but names no one. Geert visited Leo in 1959. Steven Fenves, a 13-year-old Hungarian-Yugoslav Jewish boy in the same column, later became an engineering professor in the US. His USHMM oral history is how we know what happened next.
Berlstedt, 8–10 April 1945

“Whatever you do, stall.”

  • A prisoner from the Buchenwald camp resistance passes the word: the main camp is being emptied, prisoners loaded into open rail cars.
  • Three men hide in the brick kilns overnight. The morning count is short, and the column loses most of a day.
  • 10 Apr They climb the hill to Buchenwald. “On that day there were no more transports out.”
  • 11 Apr The US Army arrives. Buchenwald is liberated.
[14:30 · ~40s] After eight days they reach Berlstedt, a brickworks camp that supplied Buchenwald. SS from Buchenwald take over the column, and with them is a prisoner in the red beret of the camp resistance. He tells Fenves: "Whatever you do, stall. Buchenwald is being emptied." Three men hide in the kilns. The SS have to deliver a head count, so the column stands for most of a day while guards search. Then gunfire is heard from the west for the first time and the SS march them out. They arrive on the 10th. The crematorium chimney is cold, the camp resistance controls the gate, no more transports leave. The next afternoon the Americans arrive. A day earlier and they'd have been loaded onto a train to somewhere else.
May 1945

“Am well and healthy.”

  • About four weeks in liberated Buchenwald, with Leo Palache and Anton Schepen.
  • 9 May Red Cross message from Eindhoven to Johanna: “Am well and healthy. Know nothing of the family. Was in Buchenwald.”
  • 12 May Home in Rotterdam, “unrecognisable”.
[15:10 · ~30s] Check against your outline: there is no field hospital in the records. He stayed in Buchenwald about four weeks after liberation (a note of 3 May lists Greydanus, Schepen, Palache for a medical examination), was trucked to the Eindhoven reception centre on 8–9 May, and sent this Red Cross message. Home on 12 May with teeth missing, back at work two days later. He was bitter about how the force treated him afterwards. In August 1947 his son Jaap, conscripted, was killed in a friendly-fire incident in the Dutch East Indies. In September 1947 the family sailed for Canada. He farmed near Clinton, Ontario, and died there in 1965. Pause here for questions.

Questions?

About Geert, before we talk about how this got pieced together.

jared-dykstra.github.io/geert-greydanus

[15:40 · ~2 min] Take questions about the story. Leave the QR code up while you take them, so people can open the site on their phones. Keep it to two minutes; the AI part is still to come. Likely questions and short answers: — Did he go on the Jehovah's Witness raid? Unknown. The memo is undated and unsigned. — Was he recognised by Yad Vashem? Jurjen Hoekstra submitted a proposal in 2020; it was not accepted. Leo Palache's own testimony doesn't name Geert. — What happened to Markus? Life sentence in 1949, cut to 18 years. — Where are the originals? Family papers; plus Arolsen, NIOD, the US National Archives, Delpher newspapers.
Intersecting stories · 1

The Allied airmen “helper” files

  • After the war the US Army asked every Dutch helper of downed airmen to fill in a questionnaire.
  • 4 Jan 1944 B-17 bombardier Ford W. Babcock is brought to the Satter farm.
  • Hendrik Satter: “Hiding the pilot was the cause of my arrest.”
  • Geert isn't named in any of them. Each helper listed only other airman-helpers.
[17:40 · ~30s] A completely separate archive: the US Army's 1945–46 files on Dutch citizens proposed for awards for helping American airmen. Jo Satter's form says it plainly: on 4 January 1944 two marechaussees brought the American flyer Ford William Babcock to the farm. His father Hendrik wrote that hiding the pilot was the cause of his arrest. The forms name Theo van Braak, the teacher Geert helped with pilots in March 1944. They never name Geert. Is that because he wasn't involved, or because each helper only listed fellow airman-helpers, and Geert's own forms describe him as a policeman in hiding? You can only ask that question when both archives sit side by side.
Intersecting stories · 2

The Gerstein report, under a roof tile

  • Kurt Gerstein, an SS officer, saw the gas chambers at Belzec in 1942 and begged a Dutch friend to get word to London.
  • 25 Mar 1943 A Trouw courier writes it out on the Satter farm: “Killing installations in Poland.”
  • “Put it away in the chicken coop.” It stayed there the whole year Geert hid on the farm.
  • Two weeks later, in Rotterdam, Geert refused to round up Jews.
[18:10 · ~40s] (It's Gerstein, with an e-i.) One of the first eyewitness accounts of the gas chambers was written out in the Satter farmhouse on 25 March 1943 by Cor van der Hooft, a Trouw distributor, with Hendrik and Jo Satter watching. They feared a trap, and wanted to get the SS officer and his family into hiding before publishing. Jo said: put it in the chicken coop. Van der Hooft never came back for it; he was arrested in April 1944 and later shot by the SD. It lay under a roof tile until after the war. A near-identical copy did reach the Dutch government in London in April 1943, and was never published. The Gerstein report is the one cited at Nuremberg, PS-1553. No source says Geert saw it or knew it was there; he was kept out of the Trouw meetings, on purpose. But it's the same farm, the same year, and the same fate he refused to take part in. I photographed that coop in 2023 before I knew any of this.
Takeaway

I lobbed a mess at Claude. It found the graph.

People, places, dates and documents, cross-checked across Dutch, German and English. Not possible for me without AI.

[18:50 · ~40s] This is the real takeaway. I didn't organise anything first. I gave Claude the scans, the half-transcriptions, the family interview, the links, and asked it to make sense of it. What it did is graph work: every person, place, date and document becomes a node, and the value is in the edges. A Red Cross form names a man; a German newspaper notice has his death sentence; a museum page has his cell; a US Army form ties the same farm to an airman. It read the Dutch, the German and the handwriting, and it kept track of which source said what — including where sources disagree, which the site shows side by side instead of picking one. I could never have done this cross-referencing alone. Not in ten years of off-and-on, and I tried.
Takeaway

I didn't need the wall anymore. No strings, no arrows, no sticky notes.

The structure I used to build by hand, before I could even start, is now something I ask for when I need it.

[19:30 · ~20s] The inset is the wall from slide 12, crossed out. The wall was never the goal. It was scaffolding I needed because I couldn't hold it all in my head. That scaffolding is gone. I didn't have to design a schema, or a database, or a filing system first. The model held the mess, and gave me structure on demand: a timeline, a map, a people table, a list of conflicts.

“What contradictions are there?”
“What should we research next?”
[19:50 · ~40s] Demystify it. The "website" is a GitHub repository: folders of documents, and one central HTML file that Claude edits. GitHub Pages publishes it. Every change is a commit, so the whole research history is there, version by version. There's no application. The only scripts are small helpers Claude wrote to print the page as a PDF and draw the map (in tools/). If someone asks "is there code?", that's the honest answer. The work is the prompts. Not "build me a page", but questions: What contradictions are there? What should we research next? Which of these two men called "Oom Gert" is Geert? The answers come back as edits, with a source cited for every claim.
Takeaway

We're used to working inside rigid structures

  • Frameworks and tools that walk work from one state to the next.
  • Tickets, schemas, PRs and code reviews, relational databases.
  • They exist because we were the bottleneck.
  • It's time to strip them back and ask which ones still earn their place.
[19:50 · ~30s] Our tools encode an assumption: that the human reading, sorting and checking is the scarce resource. So we force messy reality into rigid shapes early: a ticket template, a schema, a review gate. Be honest if asked: this project still used 27 pull requests. Some structure stays. The question isn't "throw it all away", it's "which of these exist only because we used to be the bottleneck?" Let me show you what it looks like when a whole civilisation misses a shift like this.

Where is this clock?

[20:05 · ~30s] Ask, then wait. Expect phones out again: Google Lens or an AI app will get it in seconds. That's the callback to the memo at the start. Answer: the Torre dell'Orologio on St Mark's Square, Venice. Advance once someone has it.
St Mark's Square, Venice

When was this clock finished?

  • And what year did Columbus sail?
  • And what year did Copernicus publish the heliocentric model?
[20:20 · ~30s] Ask all three questions. Let people guess, or Google. (Columbus 1492; Copernicus, De revolutionibus, 1543.) The clock in the Torre dell'Orologio shows the hours on a 24-hour ring, the zodiac, the sun and the phases of the moon. The original 1499 dial also tracked five planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury) on concentric circles. They were removed in the 1750s, when Bartolomeo Ferracina rebuilt the mechanism (from 1752): the planetary gearing was highly complex and was hurting the clock's timekeeping, so the dial was cut back to the zodiac and the phases of the moon. The old worldview was literally taken out of the clock because it got in the way of keeping time. Its model of the heavens was Ptolemaic: Earth at the centre, everything turning around us. (Your outline said heliocentric; it's the other way round, and that helps the point.) Venice was the gateway between Europe and the eastern trade routes, at the peak of its power, and it built a monument to its picture of the universe.
The answer

Venice finished its clock just as the world turned

1492
Columbus sails west.
1498
Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea, around Venice instead of through it.
1499
The clock is unveiled, tracking the planets around an Earth-centred universe.

The world didn't stop. But everything was re-oriented.

[20:50 · ~40s] Columbus 1492. Vasco da Gama reaches India by sea in 1498, so spices can reach Europe without passing through Venice. The tower is inaugurated in 1499. Forty-four years later Copernicus moves the sun to the centre. The Venetians weren't foolish; they were the best in the world at the old game, inside a worldview that made perfect sense. They never imagined what would change. And trade didn't stop. It re-oriented, west across the Atlantic instead of east to the Levant, and the centre of gravity moved to Lisbon, Seville, Antwerp and Amsterdam. (Dates: tower and clock unveiled 1 February 1499; structure attributed to Mauro Codussi, clockwork by the Rainieri family; sources give 1493 or 1495 for the commission.)

AI makes the impossible possible. It also means letting go of the frameworks that were comfortable.

  • Stop forcing a messy world into our structures first.
  • Meet the world where it is.
[21:30 · ~30s] A box of papers I couldn't read for fifteen years became a cited, public archive in about three weeks, because I stopped trying to build the wall first. The frameworks we use at work — PRs, code review, relational schemas, the process that moves work from state to state — exist because of a worldview where we were the bottleneck. That worldview is ending. The work doesn't stop. It re-orients. Close by pointing back to the memo in their hands: one sheet of paper, a P.S. about coffee, and a whole life behind it that a machine helped me read.

Thank you
